patent: Filed March 5, 1954 and issued February 5, 1957 to Daryl M. Chapin, Calvin S. Fuller and Gerald L. Pearson of Bell Telephone Laboratories. It covers the Bell silicon solar cell, generally regarded as the first practical solar cell, which the three inventors described in "A New Silicon p-n Junction Photocell for Converting Solar Radiation into Electrical Power" (Journal of Applied Physics, vol. 25, p. 676, 1954). The cell is a thick n-type silicon wafer wrapped in a very thin, heavily doped p-type skin made by diffusing boron from the vapor, with both contacts plated on the back so the front stays open to light (FIG. 1). The text claims efficiencies above five percent, against about one percent for earlier converters. The intended use, a string of cells charging a storage battery through a blocking diode (FIG. 2) to run remote repeaters on rural carrier telephone lines, shapes the claims: claims 1-3 and 10 recite the battery-charging arrangement, the rest the cell, alone or in series with utilization means. The boron diffusion process is the subject of Fuller's companion application filed the same day (Serial No. 414,272).

figs.1: Cross section of one cell, layer thicknesses not to scale: the text gives about 0.1 mil for p-type layer 13 against about 40 mils for n-type zone 12. The outer band hatched in the opposite direction is the p layer; it wraps the whole n body (letters p and n) except in the middle of the back face, where it is etched away (the step at 15) and n-contact strip 17 sits in the gap. The same heavy-dash hatching marks polystyrene coating 20 on the front and the wax seals 21 and 22 that separate strip 17 from the p layer. Strips 18 and 19, plated on the p layer at either end of the back, are the positive terminals. The sunlight arrows end at the front face 14 of the p layer, so light reaches the junction through coating 20 and the thin p layer; 10 (underlined) denotes the whole cell.
figs.2: Circuit of the charging arrangement. Each box is one cell 10 drawn as its p and n zones; they are wired p to n, so their voltages add (series-aiding), and the broken line stands for any number of further cells. The p end of the string is the positive output; it feeds the + terminal of battery 30 through diode 31, whose triangle points toward the battery, so charging current passes and the battery cannot discharge back through dark cells. Load 32 is connected directly across the battery and draws from it whether or not the cells are lit.

glossary.def: The boundary between p-type and n-type regions of one crystal. Its built-in field separates electron-hole pairs made by absorbed light, which drives current through an external circuit.
Semiconductor doped so that conduction is mainly by electrons (n) or by holes (p). Boron makes silicon p-type.
A device that turns light directly into electrical power through a junction, with no heat cycle; today called a solar cell.
The less numerous carrier type in a region: electrons in p-type material, holes in n-type.
The average distance a minority carrier travels before it recombines. Carriers generated farther than this from the junction are mostly lost, hence the thin front layer.
Bulk resistance of a material, independent of shape; lower values mean heavier doping. The p layer here is about 100 times less resistive than the n body.
Heating silicon in a boron-bearing gas (boron trichloride here) so boron atoms enter the surface and convert a thin outer layer to p-type.
A metal contact with low, linear resistance rather than rectifying behavior.

Bare silicon reflects roughly a third of incident sunlight. A transparent layer whose index is near the geometric mean of the two media on either side cuts this loss; with the right thickness this is the modern antireflection coating.
The patent's spelling of rectangular parallelepiped, a rectangular block.
Sources connected so that their voltages add.
A rectifier that passes current one way only; used here as what is now called a blocking diode.
A semiconductor diode, as distinct from a vacuum-tube diode.
Cell voltage with no current drawn; about 0.52 volt per cell here, which is why cells are stacked in series to charge a battery.
Telephone lines on which several conversations share one pair of wires on separate carrier frequencies, with amplifying repeater stations along the route.
One thousandth of an inch, 25.4 micrometres.
